sentences.t: Brothers Kumar and Sekar Vembu with Shailesh Kumar start contract software work in East Tambaram, Chennai; Tony Thomas starts a parallel operation in New Jersey writing a Java library for the SNMP protocol (Zoho's 25-years blog, 2021).
He prints 'VP of Marketing and Business Development, Advent Network Management' cards for $10 at Office Depot and staffs a 10x10 booth at the Networld+Interop show in Las Vegas.
Sales that year: $350,000, all ploughed back (Zoho blog).
Sales cross $1 million in 1998 and triple in 2000 towards $10 million.
Sridhar becomes CEO in 2000 after a year of resisting Tony Thomas's push (Zoho blog).
A venture capitalist offers $10 million for a 5% stake.
The founders decline, judging the telecom market will shrink, not grow (Zoho's surviving-the-crisis blog, 2008).
The telecom bubble bursts; by 2003 over 90% of the equipment makers AdventNet supplied in 1999-2000 are out of business.
Banked cash from 2000 funds the pivot: ManageEngine in 2002-03 and Zoho.com in 2005 (Zoho blog).
The company starts hiring class-12 graduates from low-income homes and training them in-house; about 15% of staff now come through what became Zoho Schools (Forbes India, 2016; Zoho).
The US company with an India development centre becomes an Indian company; Pleasanton, California stays the sales-facing global headquarters (Forbes India, 2016).
Girish Mathrubootham, then vice president of product management, quits to found Freshdesk, later Freshworks, the first of several funded startups by Zoho alumni (Forbes India, 2016).
FY22 revenue reaches ₹6,711 crore.
In September 2023 Zoho announces 100 million users across 55-plus applications (entrackr; Business Standard).
Vembu becomes chief scientist in January 2025, handing the group CEO role to Shailesh Kumar Davey.
Zoho launches its own Zia LLM stack in July 2025.
FY25 revenue hits ₹12,313 crore but profit dips 3%.
On 13 October 2026 Vembu announces a salary-freeze year (moneycontrol; entrackr; Mint; Indian Express).
Sridhar Vembu's origin story is often told from the village, so let us do that quickly and correctly.
He was born in 1968 in Umayalpuram, a village in Tamil Nadu's Kaveri delta famous for a mridangam maestro who happened to be his mother's cousin.
His father worked in the Madras High Court.

Vembu topped his class-12 exams, ranked 27th in the IIT Joint Entrance Examination, went to IIT Madras, then to Princeton for a PhD in electrical engineering, and then did something his degree was not for: in April 1996, in Silicon Valley, he tried to build hardware, blew his life savings, and took a contract job fixing obscure bugs in pre-ANSI C code at a company that had been absorbed by Cisco.
'I had already made up my mind I would never ever use my PhD to get a job,' he wrote years later.
'I wanted to work in the trenches of software' (25-years blog, 2021).
The company he would run was already forming without him.
In East Tambaram, a Chennai suburb, his brothers Kumar and Sekar had started a contract software outfit with Shailesh Kumar, who still heads Zoho's engineering.

In New Jersey, Tony Thomas, three years Vembu's senior at IIT and working at AT&T Bell Labs, had started a bedroom operation in 1995, helped by a personal loan from his elder brother Joy, writing a Java library for the SNMP protocol that telecom equipment makers use to manage networks.
A common friend from IIT introduced Vembu to Thomas; Vembu introduced Thomas to his brothers.
The two halves began working together in mid-to-late 1996 (25-years blog).
Vembu's entry into the firm is the scene to remember.
In early 1997, Thomas came to Silicon Valley to sell his SNMP software and asked Vembu, over lunch, if he knew anyone who could help.
He could not pay anything.
Vembu offered himself.

There was no job to join, so he manufactured one: he printed business cards for $10 at Office Depot reading 'VP of Marketing and Business Development, Advent Network Management', and staffed the 10x10 booth Thomas had rented at Networld+Interop in Las Vegas.
'To my own surprise and Tony's surprise, I made some sales at that event,' he wrote.
'I was not a good salesman...
but then Tony was even worse than me, so by the law of comparative advantage I became the salesman.' Sales in 1997 came to $350,000.
Every dollar went back into R&D for the next product, Web NMS.

In 1998, sales crossed $1 million and the founders began paying themselves modest salaries; Vembu declared the company 'a real business' only then, because it could put food on the table (25-years blog).
By 1999-2000, AdventNet was selling network-management software into the biggest bubble most of its customers would ever see.

The telecom equipment boom was, in Vembu's accounting, bigger than the dotcom bubble the media watched: over a trillion dollars eventually written off between carrier debt and venture capital into equipment startups.

He had an unusual vantage point: 'I personally must have visited 80% of those equipment companies, as a software supplier.' He had also read his history, the Japanese bubble of the late 1980s, and he could hear the same pitch repeated by dozens of companies that did not know the others existed (surviving-the-crisis blog, 2008).
In 2000, a venture capitalist offered AdventNet $10 million for a 5% stake, a $200 million valuation for a company heading towards $10 million in sales.
The partners turned it down.
'We felt the industry was going to shrink, not grow, and we didn't want to commit to a growth projection when our instinct told us to get ready for contraction,' Vembu wrote.
'One of my friends in venture capital did tell me I was a fool - but that folly saved us.' They did something else that mattered just as much: they did not let headcount chase revenue.
'We simply banked the cash - which came in really handy in the subsequent nuclear winter.' (2008 blog.)
The winter was worse than he imagined.
Vembu thought perhaps 20% of the startups would survive; in the event, he reckons three out of more than 200 did.
By 2003, over 90% of the companies AdventNet had supplied in 1999-2000 were gone.
What saved the company was the boring sequence: no outside money to answer to, cash in the bank, young engineers on payroll.

The reinvention came in two steps: ManageEngine, IT-management software for companies rather than equipment makers, born in 2002-03, and Zoho.com, rented business software delivered over the internet, in 2005.
'Indeed, it was that cash that enabled us to diversify in 2004, and that was ultimately what led to Zoho' (2008 blog; 25-years blog).
There is a second, quieter refusal in the record.
Some fifteen years before his Forbes India interview in 2016, the one time Vembu entertained a VC term sheet, he read the clause requiring a guaranteed exit or liquidity within seven or eight years.
'There was no way I could guarantee that,' he said.
His summary of the whole philosophy: 'Why sacrifice freedom?
That is the primary reason.
We operate on our own clock' (Forbes India, 2016).
In 2005, the company began an experiment that looks, in hindsight, like its most consequential product.
It started hiring teenagers straight out of class 12 from low-income households and training them in-house to build software.
The programme became Zoho University, now Zoho Schools.
Paramasivam Saran Babu, one of six recruits in the first batch, was trying to finish school at a government 'corporation school' in Chennai while his diabetic father ran a printing press.
'I hardly spoke any English at the time, but I was really good at math...
maybe that's why they hired me,' he told Forbes India.

Eleven years later he was the product manager for Zoho Creator, a low-code product used from the SRM University next door to the Napa Valley Film Festival, with a team of 30 under him and 60 collaborators (Forbes India, 2016).
The idea was never charity; it was a hiring thesis.
'Formal education only takes you so far, but most of the contextual knowledge comes from actually doing something,' Vembu said.

About 15% of the company's employees now come through Zoho Schools, and the company says it is expanding the model to more students, new disciplines and international branches (Forbes India, 2016; Zoho's Our Story page).
The same instinct, value in the overlooked, explains the geography.
From 2019 the company began breaking its big-campus model into small 'spoke' offices in towns and villages, and in 2021 it said it would hire up to 2,000 people for rural offices (Mint, 2021).
Vembu himself moved to Tenkasi, a town in Tamil Nadu's far south, and runs much of his work from there.
Zoho's operating doctrine reads like a list of things the technology industry considers impossible.
It has never raised external capital.
It says it will not go public and will not be acquired.
It runs its own data centres rather than renting the public cloud.
It claims to spend twice as much on R&D as on sales and marketing.
It has never sold customer data or shown a third-party ad inside its products, and it removed third-party trackers from its own websites.
'When you think of an operating system, you think of something that runs your device.
Zoho has software that runs your business,' Vembu told reporters in 2016 (Our Story; Forbes India, 2016).
The doctrine has a balance sheet attached to it.

Revenue went from about $200 million in 2012 (a Bloomberg interview cited by Forbes India) to ₹6,711 crore in FY22 and ₹12,313 crore in FY25, roughly a doubling in three years, with profits every year.
The FY25 split: the Zoho business-applications suite contributed 57% of revenue at ₹7,051 crore, ManageEngine 39% at ₹4,863 crore, and services the remaining ₹399 crore.
North America is still the biggest market at 41% of revenue (₹5,028 crore), followed by Asia at 30% and Europe at 23%.
The company passed 100 million users across more than 55 applications in September 2023 (entrackr; moneycontrol; Business Standard, 2023).
The family around the company matters to how it runs.
Brother Kumar, who came back to India in 1997 as president and COO for six years, later founded retail-software maker GoFrugal.
Brother Sekar runs Vembu Technologies.
Sister Radha runs Zoho Mail; the youngest sibling, Manikandan, is chief operating officer.
Tony Thomas, the first CEO, moved out in 2004 but retains his stake.
'He was the superstar in our family,' Radha Vembu says of Sridhar (Forbes India, 2016).
The strongest evidence that Zoho's training culture works is the list of people who left.

Girish Mathrubootham joined as a pre-sales engineer in 2001, rose to vice president of product management running ManageEngine, and quit in 2010 to found Freshdesk, the helpdesk startup that became Freshworks and eventually listed on Nasdaq, laying off 11% of its staff in May 2026 as it restructured for AI, a fate Zoho has so far avoided.

Other alumni: the founders of Zarget (website testing, backed by Accel and Matrix), of Voonik (fashion e-commerce), and a cluster of Chennai SaaS founders who call themselves, only half-joking, the Zoho mafia.
'The answer is very, very clear in my mind - it was the operational freedom,' Mathrubootham said of what Zoho gave him.
Matrix Partners' Tarun Davda backed Zarget largely on that pedigree: 'Zoho is a great training ground' (Forbes India, 2016; Mint, 2026).
The comparison the alumni story invites is instructive.
Freshworks raised venture money, went public, and answers to a stock price; Zoho stayed private, and answers to its own clock.

In the AI squeeze of 2026, the two Chennai schools are running the same experiment with different constraints: Freshworks cut jobs to protect a margin the market watches, while Zoho froze pay and marketing to protect a workforce nobody can force it to cut (Mint, 14 October 2026).
Every crisis in this story has arrived from the same direction: a technology shift that changed what customers would pay for.
Telecom in 2001.
Cloud in 2005.
Now AI.

Zoho saw this one early enough to build: in July 2025 it launched its own foundational model stack, Zia LLM, alongside prebuilt agents, a custom agent builder and speech-recognition models, all run on its own data centres, extending a privacy argument (your data, our metal) into the AI era (Indian Express, July 2025).

The consumer bet followed: Arattai ('chit-chat' in Tamil), a homegrown messaging app, went viral last year and hit the number one spot on Indian app stores; on 2 October 2026, a day after Meta started charging businesses for certain WhatsApp service messages, Zoho launched Arattai for business, free for government and public services like the Railways, with a million free messages a month for healthcare and educational institutions (India Today, 2 October 2026).
And yet the same fortnight brought the most telling moment in the company's recent history.
On 13 October 2026, Vembu posted on X: 'We have cut down on our marketing budget.
We have also told our employees that we cannot have our usual pay increase this year.
I have apologized for not being able to avoid this.
We will work hard to avoid mass layoffs but the outlook for software jobs in general is grim.
We have not been growing our employee count for 18 months now.' He cited a four-fold increase in server prices for AI data centres and a difficult geopolitical backdrop (Mint, 14 October 2026).
The financials show the squeeze arriving in two waves.
In FY23, the year generative AI went mainstream, profit rose 3% but employee costs jumped 49%.

In FY25, employee costs rose another 29% to ₹4,347 crore, advertising spend rose 31.3% to ₹2,230 crore, depreciation nearly half-again to ₹741 crore as data-centre investment bit, and net profit slipped 3% to ₹3,191 crore on revenue up 17.8% to ₹12,313 crore.
The company still spends only ₹0.75 to earn each rupee of revenue, holds ₹1,880 crore of cash, and runs a 31.27% EBITDA margin.
This is not distress.
It is a margin decision being made early, by choice, which is the whole point of being Zoho (moneycontrol; entrackr; Mint).
What did the company get wrong?
Two things are defensible criticisms, not hindsight.
First, it hired ahead of the shift: a 49% jump in employee costs in FY23 was a bet that the SaaS expansion would continue, and the 18-month headcount freeze is the admission that it did not.
Second, its moat is also its exposure.

Zoho's low-price suite sells to small businesses, and consultants note that small clients with little custom data are exactly the customers who can migrate fastest when AI makes cheap internal automation possible.
'Many of its clients are small clients, who aren't too reliant on custom data - and may thus migrate rapidly to cost-effective solutions due to AI,' says YCP India's Abhisek Mukherjee.
The counter is 29 years of reinvention: the company that sells the 'operating system for business' is betting it can also be the company that supplies the agents (Mint, 14 October 2026).
The decision scene belongs to Shailesh Kumar Davey, the engineer from the East Tambaram room who became group CEO in January 2025.

His inheritance is precise: keep the ₹3,191 crore profit engine funding the AI build-out, hold the 30,000-strong workforce together without the layoffs peers have chosen, and prove that a bootstrapped Indian company can own its models, its data centres and its pricing power at once.
Vembu, now chief scientist, has moved himself to the R&D problem that decides it.
The company that refused the cheque in 2000 is placing the same bet again: that it is better to be early, own the downside, and answer to no one.
